arch-support.name: Arch support
arch-support.description:
Neutral / cushion / high arch

Shoes for runners who do not need any additional arch support (Around 50% of runners). Best for people with normal, high or medium high arches. See the best neutral shoes.

Stability / overpronation / normal arch

Shoes for runners who need mild to moderate arch support (Around 45% of runners). Best for runners with a low arch. See the best stability shoes.

Motion control / severe overpronation / flat feet

Shoes for runners who needs a lot of arch support. Best for runners with flat feet. See the best motion control shoes.

Good to know

- Rule of thumb: If in doubt, buy neutral shoes to avoid injuries.
- More about arch support in this video.
- Find your arch type by following steps from this video.

arch-type.name: Arch Type
arch-type.description:
High arch

High arch means that there is a visible "arch" on the inner side of your foot. Shoes for runners with high arches don't have any supportive features. They are also known as neutral running shoes.

Low arch

Also refers to flat feet, when there is a very minimal "arch" or the foot lays flat on the floor. Shoes for low arches help to support the foot and correct the gait. These include stability and motion control shoes.

Not sure about your arch type? Follow the "wet test" in our guide.

features.name: Features
features.description:
Carbon fiber plate

Used in elite running shoes (like Nike Vapofly) to enhance speed. The plate is placed inside the midsole to create a springboard-like effect. Learn more in our guide on carbon plates.

Rocker

Rocker-bottom running shoes have a rounded midsole geometry that mimics the motion of a rocking chair. This design helps to speed up the heel-to-toe transition and save runner's energy. Learn more in our guide on rockered shoes.

Rock plate

Embedded into the midsole, a stiff rock plate helps to protect the foot from sharp rocks and debris outdoors.

Orthotic friendly/Removable insole

Shoes with easily removable insoles that can be replaced with custom inserts or orthotics.

Slip-On

Shoes that can be slipped on and off without the need to use laces.

Sockless wear

Shoes with soft and breathable uppers that feel comfortable when worn without socks. Often necessary for triathlon.

heel-to-toe-drop.name: Heel to toe drop
heel-to-toe-drop.description:
The height difference from the heel to the forefoot, also known as heel drop, toe spring, heel to toe spring or simply drop.

There are many opinions about what a good heel drop is. We do not recommend any in particular. Lean more in this video.

pronation.name: Pronation
pronation.description:
Pronation is the degree to which your foot and ankle roll inward.

It can be neutral (more or less straight), excessively rolling inwards (overpronation) or outwards (underpronation/supination).

Learn more about pronation types in our guide.

season.name: Season
season.description:
Summer

Highly breathable shoes for temperatures above 60°F (15°C).

Winter

Warm, less breathable shoes for temperatures below 50°F (10°C). Some of the shoes are also waterproof.

strike-pattern.name: Strike Pattern
strike-pattern.description:
If in doubt, choose heel strike. 94% of runners are heel strikers. However, race running shoes tend to be better for midfoot/forefoot strike.

To learn more, see our guide on foot strike.

terrain.name: Terrain
terrain.description:
Road

Shoes best for road, track and light gravel. See the best road shoes.

Trail

Shoes best for trail, off road, mountains and other unstable surfaces. See the best trail shoes.

Good to know

As long as you stick to the road or path, and if you want just one running shoe, buy a road running shoe.

type.name: Type
type.description:
Cushioned

Shoes with high shock absorption (impact protection).

Comfortable

Well-cushioned and well-padded shoes that help to prevent fatigue and discomfort.

Breathable

Shoes that provide sufficient airflow for warm weather. Learn more about the role of breathability in running shoes in our guide.

Minimalist

Shoes with thinner soles (less than 16 mm) and lower drop (less than 5 mm) that promote a more natural, grounded experience.

Barefoot

The thinnest running shoes that are closest to a barefoot-like experience.

Maximalist

Highly cushioned shoes with the heel thickness of 30 mm and above. Best for long distances and recovery runs. Learn more about stack height and how it affects running performance in our in-depth research.

For heavy runners/For big guys

Generously cushioned and stable running shoes that support runners above 200 lbs (90 kg).

Lightweight

Shoes lighter than 8.8 oz (250g). Lighter shoes help to improve speed and prevent fatigue.

use.name: Use
use.description:
Jogging

Comfortable running shoes for steady and slow-paced running sessions.

Long distance

Daily running shoes with enough cushioning for distances over 10K.

For beginners

Well-cushioned, supportive, and moderately priced running shoes.

All-day wear

Running shoes that have enough cushioning and support to keep the foot comfortable for up to 10 hours straight.

Walking

Cushioned and flexible shoes that are comfortable to wear casually.

Treadmill

Cushioned road running shoes with breathable uppers that are perfect for indoor workouts.

Mud

Trail running shoes with deep lugs (about 5 mm) and an effective tread pattern that sheds off mud on the go.

Snow

Warm waterproof shoes with excellent grip.

Off-trail

Extra rugged, protective, and grippy trail running shoes for unpredictable conditions.

Hiking

More cushioned and protective trail running shoes that have enough support for a day hike with a light backpack.

Triathlon

Speed-oriented race shoes that are breathable and quick-drying.

Spartan race (OCR)

Lightweight trail runing shoes with deep lugs (5 mm) and excellent grip.

Gym

Running shoes shoes with firm and stable soles that can handle moderate strength training and lateral movements at the gym.

waterproofing.name: Waterproofing
waterproofing.description: Water-repellent shoes offer basic protection from water splashes and rain and still have some breathability. But if you want full protection, go for the waterproof options.

energy-return.name: Energy return
energy-return.description:
Energy return indicates how much of the runner's energy (%) is returned back by the shoe's sole. The higher the %, the springier the ride.

Learn more in our guide on energy return.

shock-absorption.name: Shock absorption
shock-absorption.description:
Shock absorption (SA) reflects the force absorbed by the shoe's sole. Higher SA means less impact on the runner's body.

Learn more in our guide on shock absorption.

heel-stack.name: Heel stack
heel-stack.description:
Stack height is the amount of material between your feet and the ground. For beginner runners, we recommend getting a shoe with an average stack height.

Seasoned runners can learn more in our detailed guide on stack height (includes a tool that helps you find the right stack for you).

midsole-softness.name: Midsole softness
midsole-softness.description:
Firm cushioning most often means a more stable ride.

Plush cushioning is better for long distances and recovery runs.

In the end, it comes down to personal preference. If in doubt, choose balanced.

To learn more about cushioning, see our guide on soft vs. firm shoes.

stiffness.name: Stiffness
stiffness.description:
Flexible running shoes are better for comfort, daily runs, and all-day wear.

Stiff running shoes help to improve your running performance on fast runs.

Learn more in our in-depth study on flexibility.

traction.name: Traction
traction.description:
High

Strong, dependable grip on both wet and dry surfaces.

Medium

Generally reliable on dry ground, but grip decreases on very slippery surfaces.

Low

Poor grip on wet surfaces, may slip even on smooth dry ones.

difference-in-midsole-softness-in-cold.name: Difference in midsole softness in cold
